Title: Determination of parameters for the steric mass action model—A comparison between two approaches

Abstract: The application of mechanistic modeling for the optimization of chromatographic steps increased recently due to time efficiency of algorithms and rising calculation power. In the modeling of ion exchange chromatography steps, the sorption processes occurring on adsorbent particle surfaces can be simulated with the steric mass action (SMA) model introduced by Brooks and Cramer (1992) [14]. In this paper, two approaches for the determination of SMA parameters will be carried out and discussed concerning their specific experimental effort, quality of results, method differences, reasons for uncertainties and consequences for SMA parameter determination: Approach I: estimation of SMA parameters based on gradient and frontal experiments according to instructions in Brooks and Cramer (1992) [14] and Shukla et al. (1998) [16]. Approach II: application of an inverse method for parameter estimation, resulting in SMA parameters that induce a best fit of chromatographic data to a mechanistic model for column chromatography. These approaches for SMA parameter determination were carried out for three proteins (ribonuclease A, cytochrome c and lysozyme) at pH 5 and pH 7. The results were comparable and the order of parameter values and their relations to the chromatographic data similar. Nevertheless, differences in the complexity and effort of methods as well as the parameter values themselves were observed. The comparison of methods demonstrated that discrepancies depend mainly on model

- In this context, approaches for the determination of SMA parameters based on batch experiments, like in [18,19] are interesting but not yet fully established and validated.

Model: Rapid-equilibrium SMA
Laws:
(1) [balance] The bound concentration of component i changes through adsorption from the mobile phase and desorption back into it.
(2) [definition] The adsorbent's ionic capacity is the salt-ion concentration plus the charge-weighted concentrations of bound components.
(3) [definition] The exchange-available bound salt-ion concentration is the total bound salt concentration minus the amount shielded by bound proteins.
(4) [constitutive] The SMA equilibrium relation gives the component equilibrium coefficient from its bound-to-mobile concentration ratio and the salt-to-available-site ratio raised to the component charge.
(7) [balance] The column-level mobile concentration changes through axial convection and dispersion, with mass transfer to the particles.
(8) [balance] The particle-level mobile concentration changes through exchange with the column fluid and adsorption or desorption involving the bound phase.

States (computed by the ODEs):
- q_{i}: Concentration of component i on the adsorbent surface
- c_{i}: Concentration of component i in the mobile phase on column level
- c_{p,i}: Concentration of component i in the mobile phase on particle level

Inputs (variables no law computes):
- c_{1}: Mobile-phase concentration of salt component 1
- q_{1}: Salt-ion concentration
- u_{int}: Interstitial velocity

Model-wide assumptions:
- Rapid equilibrium is assumed.

answer.description: The model describes ion-exchange chromatography of ribonuclease A, cytochrome c, and lysozyme in a packed column. It predicts mobile-phase and adsorbed concentrations in the column and particles using rapid-equilibrium SMA binding, which accounts for salt competition and steric shielding. Column transport is represented by axial convection and dispersion together with mass transfer to the particles; parameters are determined from gradient and frontal experiments or by inverse fitting to chromatographic data.
